headings.title: Definition and Overview of Antepartum Haemorrhage
headings.content: Antepartum haemorrhage (APH) is formally defined as any bleeding from or into the genital tract occurring from the 24th week of pregnancy up to the birth of the baby. In the context of Nigerian healthcare and global obstetric standards, distinguishing APH from bleeding in early pregnancy is critical because fetal viability is established around this gestational age. APH is a major obstetric emergency and a leading cause of maternal and perinatal morbidity and mortality worldwide, particularly in low-resource settings where timely access to comprehensive emergency obstetric care may be challenging. The bleeding can range from mere spotting to massive, life-threatening hemorrhage that can rapidly compromise both maternal hemodynamic stability and fetal oxygenation. Understanding the magnitude of APH helps nursing students appreciate the urgency required in clinical assessment. It is important to note that bleeding originating from the lower genital tract, such as cervical polyps or local trauma, must be differentiated from bleeding of placental origin, although all forms of vaginal bleeding post-24 weeks warrant thorough investigation. Nurses play a frontline role in identifying early warning signs, monitoring vital signs, and initiating emergency protocols to prevent adverse outcomes for both mother and baby.

headings.title: Causes and Etiology of Antepartum Haemorrhage
headings.content: The etiology of antepartum haemorrhage is multifactorial, but the two primary and most critical obstetric causes are placenta praevia and abruptio placentae (placental abruption). Placenta praevia occurs when the placenta implants partially or completely in the lower uterine segment, encroaching upon or covering the internal cervical os. Abruptio placentae involves the premature separation of a normally implanted placenta from the uterine wall before the delivery of the fetus. Together, these two conditions account for the vast majority of true APH cases. Other less common causes include vasa praevia—where fetal vessels run across the internal os unsupported by placenta or umbilical cord—marginal sinus rupture, and uterine rupture. Additionally, local lesions of the lower genital tract such as cervical carcinoma, severe cervicitis, cervical polyps, or vulvovaginal varicosities can cause bleeding that mimics or contributes to APH. Identifying the exact cause requires careful clinical history, physical examination, and diagnostic imaging like ultrasound. For nursing students, categorizing these causes helps in anticipating specific clinical presentations, such as painless bright red bleeding versus painful dark red bleeding, which directly guide nursing actions and medical interventions.

headings.title: Placenta Praevia: Classification and Clinical Features
headings.content: Placenta praevia is classified into four distinct grades based on the degree of placental encroachment over the internal cervical os. Grade I (Low-lying) means the placenta is implanted in the lower uterine segment, but its lower edge does not reach the internal os. Grade II (Marginal) indicates that the placental edge reaches the margin of the internal os but does not cover it. Grade III (Partial) occurs when the internal os is partially covered by the placenta. Grade IV (Complete or Central) means the placenta completely covers the internal os. The classic clinical feature of placenta praevia is sudden, painless, bright red vaginal bleeding, typically occurring during the third trimester as the lower uterine segment stretches and the cervix begins to efface. The bleeding is often recurrent and can be profuse without warning. Because the placenta is low-lying, abdominal examination often reveals a uterus that is soft, non-tender, and relaxed, with the fetal head frequently floating or presenting in an abnormal lie such as breech or transverse. Vaginal examination is strictly contraindicated in suspected placenta praevia unless performed in a fully equipped operating theatre due to the risk of provoking catastrophic hemorrhage. Nursing students must remember: 'No digital vaginal examination until placenta praevia is ruled out by ultrasound.'

headings.title: Abruptio Placentae: Types and Clinical Features
headings.content: Abruptio placentae, also known as placental abruption, is the premature separation of a normally situated placenta. It can be classified into revealed, concealed, or mixed types. In revealed abruption, the blood tracks down between the membranes and the uterine wall, escaping through the vagina, so the external bleeding matches the degree of shock. In concealed abruption, the blood is trapped behind the placenta, meaning external bleeding is absent or minimal, making the condition extremely dangerous because the degree of shock is disproportionately high compared to visible blood loss. Mixed abruption involves both concealed and revealed components. The clinical features of abruptio placentae typically include sudden, severe, constant abdominal or back pain, accompanied by dark red vaginal bleeding (in revealed types). The uterus is characteristically hypertonic, tender, and feels hard or board-like upon palpation. Fetal distress or demise is common due to the compromised uteroplacental blood flow. Maternal complications can rapidly escalate to disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), hemorrhagic shock, and acute kidney injury. Predisposing factors include maternal hypertension, trauma, advanced maternal age, and previous abruption. Nurses must vigilantly monitor abdominal tone, pain levels, and vital signs to detect concealed bleeding early.

headings.title: Nursing Assessment and Diagnosis in APH
headings.content: Nursing assessment and diagnosis in APH require systematic, rapid, and calm action. Upon admission of a patient with APH, the nurse must immediately assess airway, breathing, and circulation (the ABCs) while simultaneously gathering a targeted history. Key assessment parameters include estimating the amount and color of vaginal bleeding, inquiring about the presence and nature of abdominal pain or contractions, and checking fetal movements. Vital signs—blood pressure, pulse rate, respiratory rate, and oxygen saturation—must be baseline-assessed and monitored frequently to detect early signs of hypovolemic shock. Palpation of the abdomen must be done gently, noting uterine tenderness, tone (soft versus board-like), and fetal lie or presentation. Vaginal examinations must be avoided until ultrasound localization of the placenta is confirmed. Essential diagnostic investigations ordered in collaboration with the medical team include a full blood count (checking hemoglobin and hematocrit), blood grouping and cross-matching (reserving at least 2 to 4 units of compatible blood), coagulation profile (fibrinogen, PT, APTT to rule out DIC), and renal function tests. Continuous or intermittent electronic fetal monitoring is crucial to assess fetal well-being. Nursing diagnoses commonly formulated include deficient fluid volume related to hemorrhage, risk for ineffective tissue perfusion, acute pain related to uterine trauma or stretching, and anxiety related to the perceived threat to maternal and fetal survival.

headings.title: Emergency Nursing Management and Resuscitation
headings.content: Emergency nursing management of APH focuses on stabilizing the mother, maintaining tissue perfusion, and preparing for prompt delivery if indicated. The nurse must immediately insert two large-bore intravenous (IV) cannulas (16G or 18G) to facilitate rapid fluid resuscitation with crystalloids, such as normal saline or Ringer's lactate, and subsequent blood transfusion. Oxygen therapy via face mask is administered to optimize maternal and fetal oxygenation. Blood samples must be drawn immediately for baseline labs, including cross-matching and coagulation studies. Continuous monitoring of vital signs, urine output via an indwelling urinary catheter (aiming for a minimum output of 30 mL/hour), and accurate pad counts or weighing of blood-soaked linens are vital nursing responsibilities. The nurse must keep the patient and family informed, offering reassurance while mobilizing the multidisciplinary team—including obstetricians, anesthesiologists, and pediatricians. Preparation for emergency delivery (either via Cesarean section or vaginal delivery depending on the severity of hemorrhage, gestational age, and cause) must be carried out swiftly. For abruption with DIC, administration of fresh frozen plasma, platelets, or cryoprecipitate may be required. Clear communication, precise charting, and adherence to emergency obstetric protocols are hallmarks of effective nursing care.

headings.title: Maternal and Fetal Complications
headings.content: Antepartum haemorrhage carries significant maternal and fetal risks that demand vigilant nursing observation. Maternal complications include hemorrhagic shock, which can progress to multiple organ dysfunction syndrome if inadequately managed. Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is particularly associated with severe placental abruption due to the release of tissue thromboplastin into the maternal circulation. Other potential maternal complications encompass acute kidney injury resulting from prolonged renal hypoperfusion, emergency hysterectomy to control intractable postpartum hemorrhage, operative complications from emergency Cesarean sections, and psychological trauma such as postpartum anxiety or post-traumatic stress disorder. Fetal complications are equally severe and include chronic or acute fetal hypoxia, fetal distress, intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) due to inadequate placental perfusion, premature birth with its attendant respiratory distress syndrome and neonatal intensive care unit admission, and perinatal death (stillbirth or early neonatal death). Understanding these potential complications enables nursing students to anticipate urgent clinical needs, advocate for timely interventions, and provide empathetic, comprehensive post-crisis support to grieving or traumatized families.

headings.title: Health Education and Preventive Care for Pregnant Women
headings.content: Health education and preventive care form the cornerstone of reducing the incidence and severity of antepartum haemorrhage, particularly within community health settings in Nigeria. Antenatal care (ANC) attendance is crucial; nurses must educate pregnant women on the importance of early and regular booking visits to screen for risk factors such as previous uterine surgery, high parity, advanced maternal age, and hypertensive disorders. Pregnant women should be thoroughly educated on danger signs during pregnancy, specifically warning them that any vaginal bleeding—no matter how painless or small in amount—requires immediate reporting to a healthcare facility rather than waiting for their scheduled appointment. Health talks should emphasize lifestyle modifications, including avoidance of abdominal trauma, cessation of smoking and substance use, and strict adherence to prescribed antihypertensive medications for women with chronic hypertension or preeclampsia. Community sensitization programs can help dispel cultural myths surrounding bleeding in pregnancy, encouraging women to seek orthodox medical care promptly. Furthermore, nurses should counsel women who have experienced APH regarding future reproductive health and the signs to watch for in subsequent pregnancies.
